<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:statement}
The commuting scheme $\mathcal{C}_K$ is Cohen-Macaulay and normal (thus, reduced) when $K$ is an arbitrary field of characteristic $0$. Furthermore, its Hilbert series is given by $H(t)(1-t)^{-16}$ where:
\[H(t):=1 + 12t + 64t^2 + 198t^3 + 388t^4 + 492t^5 + 395t^6 + 198t^7 + 64t^8 + 12t^9 + t^{10}.\]
In particular, the degree of $\mathcal{C}_K$ is $H(1)=1825$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
The commuting scheme $\mathcal{C}_K$ of $\mathfrak{g}_2$ defined over a field $K$ is the closed subscheme of $\mathfrak{g}_2\times \mathfrak{g}_2$ defined by the vanishing of the Lie bracket on $\mathfrak{g}_2$. More precisely, we define $\mathcal{C}_K:=\operatorname{Spec}(\mathcal{A}_K)$, where
\[\mathcal{A}_K:=\frac{K[x_1,x_2,\dots, x_{14},y_1, y_2, \dots, y_{14}]}{\Big(\sum\limits_{i,j=1}^{14}c_{i,j}^kx_iy_j: 1\leq k\leq 14\Big)}.\]
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:killing}
We have the following identities in $\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$:
\[\sum_{k,l=1}^{14}\kappa(b_k,b_l)x_k Q_l(x,y)=0,\]
\[\sum_{k,l=1}^{14}\kappa(b_k,b_l)y_k Q_l(x,y)=0.\]
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The above identities are respectively equivalent to the equalities $\kappa(x,[x,y])=0$ and $\kappa(y,[x,y])=0$, which are immediate from the invariance of the Killing form.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:genci}
We have the following identities in $\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$:
\[-\Delta Q_1(x,y)=\sum_{l=3}^{14}(\lambda_l\mu_2-\lambda_2\mu_l)Q_l(x,y),\]
\[\Delta Q_2(x,y)=\sum_{l=3}^{14}(\lambda_l\mu_1-\lambda_1\mu_l)Q_l(x,y)\]
where $\Delta=\lambda_1\mu_2-\lambda_2\mu_1$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The above corollary has the following geometric interpretation: In the coordinate ring of the basic open subscheme $\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}$ of $\mathcal{C}$ characterized by $\Delta\neq 0$, it follows that the polynomials $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ lie in the ideal generated by $Q_i$'s for $3\leq i\leq 14$. Thus, the commuting ideal is generated by these $12$ polynomials, and since $28-12=16=\dim(\mathcal{C})=\dim(\mathcal{C}_{\Delta})$, we conclude that $\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}$ is a complete intersection and that $\mathcal{C}$ is generically a complete intersection. (Note that $C_{\Delta}$ is non-empty: It contains the pair $(h_{\alpha},h_{\beta})$ where $\Delta=192$.) Thus, the two Killing-form relations above account for the discrepancy between the $14$ defining equations and the co-dimension $12$ of the commuting scheme.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:m2-first}
The quotient $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}/(\overline{s_1},\overline{s_2},\dots, \overline{s_{16}})$ is finite dimensional as an $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space. Furthermore, the Hilbert series of this quotient is
\[H(t):= 1 + 12t + 64t^2 + 198t^3 + 388t^4 + 492t^5 + 395t^6 + 198t^7 + 64t^8 + 12t^9 + t^{10}.\]
In particular, $\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}(\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}/(\overline{s_1},\overline{s_2},\dots, \overline{s_{16}}))=H(1)=1825.$
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:upper}
The elements $\{s_i\}_{1\leq i\leq 16}$ form a system of parameters for the algebra $\mathcal{A}$. Furthermore, as a $T:=\mathbb{Q}[s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16}]$-module,  $\mathcal{A}$ is generated by at most $1825$ elements.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Proposition~\ref{prop:m2-first} implies that there is a set of monomials $\overline\mathcal{B}$ in the algebra $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ such that $|\overline{\mathcal{B}}|=1825$ and their images span $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}/(\overline{s_1},\overline{s_2},\dots, \overline{s_{16}})$ as an $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space. Since there exists a surjection $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{Z}} \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$, we can lift the elements of $\overline\mathcal{B}$ to monomials in $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{Z}}$, which can then be viewed as a set of monomials $\mathcal{B}$ in $\mathcal{A}$.

Fix a non-negative integer $d$. Then, the degree $d$ component of the algebra $\mathcal{A}(0)$ is spanned by monomials in $u_i$'s of degree $d$ and is a finite dimensional vector space. Proposition~\ref{prop:m2-first} says that every monomial in the $\overline{u_i}$'s in $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ lies in the span of the elements of $\overline\mathcal{B}$ and the polynomials $\overline{P_k}(0,\overline{u_j})$. Hence, a matrix with the coefficients of the elements of $\overline\mathcal{B}$ of degree $d$ and those of the polynomials in the ideal generated by $\overline{P_k}(0,\overline{u_j})$ of degree $d$ has full column rank modulo $p$. Therefore, the same matrix with the coefficients of the elements of $\mathcal{B}$ and the degree $d$ polynomials in the ideal generated by $P_k(0,u_j)$ has full column rank, proving that every degree $d$ monomial in the $u_j$'s lies in the span of these elements. Hence, the set $\mathcal{B}$ is a spanning set for the algebra $\mathcal{A}(0)$. This proves both the claims.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
We have a graded free decomposition of $\mathcal{A}$ as a $T$-module:
\begin{align*}
\mathcal{A} \simeq T \oplus T[-1]^{12} \oplus T[-2]^{64} \oplus T[-3]^{198} \oplus T[-4]^{388}\\\oplus T[-5]^{492}\oplus T[-6]^{395}\oplus &T[-7]^{198}\oplus T[-8]^{64}\oplus T[-9]^{12}\oplus T[-10].
\end{align*}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:m2-second}
There exist polynomials $h(z), \rho_j(z)\in \mathbb{F}_p[z]$ and a linear form $\ell$ for $1\leq j\leq 12$ such that these provide a univariate parametrization for the system of equations $\overline{P_k}(\overline{c},u_j)=0$ for $1\leq k\leq 14$. In particular, the following equalities hold:
\begin{equation} \label{eq:sols}
\overline{P}_k(\overline{c},\rho_j(z))=0\text{ mod }h(z),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation} \label{eq:separate}
\ell(\rho_1(z),\rho_2(z),\dots, \rho_{12}(z))=z\text{ mod }h(z).
\end{equation}
Furthermore, these polynomials also satisfy the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The polynomial $h(z)$ has degree $1825$ and is square-free, i.e. $(h,h')=1$.
\item The GCD of $h(z)$ and the determinant of the Jacobian $\big(\frac{\partial \overline{P_i}}{\partial u_j}\big)_{3\leq i\leq 14, 1\leq j\leq 12}$ at $u_j=\rho_j(z)$ is equal to $1$.
\item The GCD of $h(z)$ with the polynomial $192(\overline{c_{15}}(\overline{c_{16}}-\overline{c_5})-\rho_1(z)(\rho_9(z)-\overline{c_{11}}))$ is equal to $1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
\item The non-zero Jacobian property in (b) of the above proposition only involves the last $12$ equations and not $\overline{P_1}$ and $\overline{P_2}$. This fact will be relevant when we lift solutions to characteristic zero below. (See Lemma~\ref{lem:Hensel}.)
\item The polynomial $192(\overline{c_{15}}(\overline{c_{16}}-\overline{c_5})-\rho_1(z)(\rho_9(z)-\overline{c_{11}}))$ in (c) is exactly the element $\Delta$ constructed in Corollary~\ref{cor:genci} after the substitution $s_i=\overline{c_i}$ and $u_j=\rho_j(z)$. This follows from the formula of $\Delta$ in terms of the $s_i$'s and $u_j$'s found in Section~\ref{sec:app1}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:finite-sol}
The system of equations $\overline{P_k}(\overline{c},u_j)=0$ for $1\leq k\leq 14$ has at least $1825$ distinct solutions in a finite extension $\mathbb{F}_{p^t}$ of $\mathbb{F}_p$ for some $t\geq 1$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Since the polynomial $h(z)$ constructed in Proposition~\ref{prop:m2-second} is square-free of degree $1825$, it has exactly $1825$ distinct roots $\{\zeta_i\}_{1\leq i\leq 1825}$ in some finite extension of $\mathbb{F}_p$. Then, using Equation~\eqref{eq:sols}, we get $1825$ distinct solutions: $(\rho_1(\zeta_i),\rho_2(\zeta_i),\cdots ,\rho_{12}(\zeta_i))$ for each $i$. The fact that these are all distinct follows from the fact that each of these solutions uniquely determines $\zeta_i$ via an application of $\ell$ as implied by Equation~\eqref{eq:separate}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:Hensel}\cite[Exercise 7.26]{Eisenbud}
Given $f_1,f_2,\dots,f_n \in R[z_1,z_2,\dots,z_n]$ where $R$ is a local ring that is complete with respect to its maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. Suppose we are given $(a_1,a_2,\dots, a_n)\in R^n$ such that $f_i(a_1,a_2,\dots, a_n) \in \mathfrak m$ for all $i$ and suppose the determinant of the Jacobian matrix $\big(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial z_j}\big)_{1\leq i,j\leq n}$ is invertible in $R$ when evaluated at the point $(a_1,a_2,\dots, a_n)$. Then, there exist $(b_1,b_2,\dots, b_n)\in R^n$ such that $f_i(b_1,b_2,\dots, b_n)=0$ for all $i$ and $b_j = a_j\mod\mathfrak{m}$ for all $j$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:Hensel}
The algebra $\mathcal{A}\otimes_T \mathcal{L}(\simeq \mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{Z}}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16}]} \mathcal{L})$ has at least $1825$ $\mathcal{F}$-valued points after scalar extension along~\eqref{eq:embedf}.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We consider the following system of equations over $\mathcal{R}$ in the variables $u_j$ for $1\leq j\leq 12$:
\[f_k(u_j):=P_k(v_i+c_i,u_j),\]
where $3\leq k\leq 14$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-sol}, this system of equations has at least $1825$ solutions modulo $\mathfrak{m}$. Therefore, using Proposition~\ref{prop:m2-second}(b) to satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:Hensel}, we can lift these to get $1825$ solutions to the system in $\mathcal{R}$. Again, by Proposition~\ref{prop:m2-second}(c) and Corollary~\ref{cor:genci}, these solutions automatically also satisfy $P_1(v_i+c_i,u_j)=P_2(v_i+c_i,u_j)=0$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{main:thm}
The algebra $\mathcal{A}$ is a free $T$-module of rank $1825$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Extending scalars via Equation~\eqref{eq:embedf}, the above proposition implies that the algebra $(\mathcal{A}\otimes_T \mathcal{L})\otimes _{\mathcal{L}} \mathcal{F} = \mathcal{A}\otimes_T \mathcal{F}$ has at least $1825$ points valued over the field $\mathcal{F}$. Evaluating at each of these points gives us a map:
\[\Phi: \mathcal{A}\otimes_T \mathcal{F} \to \mathcal{F}^{1825}.\]
By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the above map is surjective, showing that $\dim_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{A}\otimes_T \mathcal{F})\geq 1825.$ However, Corollary~\ref{cor:upper} implies that $\dim_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{A}\otimes_T \mathcal{F})\leq 1825$. This shows that $\dim_{\mathcal{F}}(\mathcal{A}\otimes_T \mathcal{F})= 1825$ and that the map $\Phi$ is an isomorphism.

By Corollary~\ref{cor:upper}, there exists a surjection of $T$-modules $\phi:T^{1825}\twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{A}$ and by the dimension argument above, the map $\phi$ becomes an isomorphism of $\mathcal{F}$-vector spaces when we tensor by $\mathcal{F}$ over $T$. Therefore, since $T^{1825}$ is torsion-free, we conclude that $\phi$ must have been an isomorphism to start with, thus proving the theorem.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:maincor}
The scheme $\mathcal{C}_K$ is reduced, Cohen-Macaulay and normal. Furthermore, the sequence $(s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16})$ is a regular sequence for $\mathcal{C}_K$ and the Hilbert series for $\mathcal{C}_K$ is given by $H(t)(1-t)^{-16}$, where $H(t)$ is the polynomial in Proposition~\ref{prop:m2-first}.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Note that $\mathcal{A}_K=\mathcal{A}\otimes_{\mathbb{Q}} K$. Therefore, Theorem~\ref{main:thm} implies that $\mathcal{A}_K$ is a free module over the polynomial ring $K[s_1,s_2,\dots,s_{16}]$. This implies that $\mathcal{C}_K$ is Cohen-Macaulay (see, for example, \cite[Corollary 18.17]{Eisenbud}). This along with generic reducedness proves that $\mathcal{C}_K$ is reduced. Finally, by \cite[Corollary 1.9(i)]{Pop08}, the scheme $\mathcal{C}_K$ is regular in codimension $1$, and so, we get that $\mathcal{C}_K$ is normal by Serre's criterion. 

That $(s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16})$ is a regular sequence for $\mathcal{C}$ follows from the fact that it is a system of parameters (by Corollary~\ref{cor:upper}) and that $\mathcal{C}$ is Cohen-Macaulay. Therefore, we conclude that the Hilbert series of $\mathcal{C}$ is $(1-t)^{-16}$ times the Hilbert series of $\mathcal{A}/(s_1,s_2,\dots,s_{16})$. The latter Hilbert series should be smaller degree-wise than the Hilbert series of the same scheme modulo $p$, since a homogeneous generating set of monomials of a given degree modulo $p$ can be lifted to $\mathbb{Z}$, and thus, to $\mathbb{Q}$. However, since the degree of the scheme modulo $p$ and in characteristic zero are both $1825$, both Hilbert series must coincide, finishing the proof. The claim for general $K$ follows from this immediately.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
\item The arguments in \cite{Pop08} are over an algebraically closed $K$, but can be extended to a general $K$ since the irregular locus of $\mathcal{C}_K$ is cut out by certain rank conditions defined over $K$ which remain unchanged when extending to $\overline K$.                                                     

\item Theorem~\ref{main:thm} above also gives a more direct proof of reducedness: Since $\mathcal{A}$ is a free $T$-module, the natural map $\mathcal{A}\to \mathcal{A}\otimes_T \mathcal{L}$ is an embedding. Hence, as $\mathcal{A}\otimes_T \mathcal{L}$ injects into $\mathcal{A} \otimes_T \mathcal{F}$, which is isomorphic to a product of fields, it is reduced and does not have any nilpotents, and therefore neither does $\mathcal{A}$. This proves reducedness of $\mathcal{C}$. Tenosring by $K$ over $\mathcal{C}$ gives reducedness of $\mathcal{C}_K$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:p-crit}
Suppose we have the dimension inequality: 
\[\dim_{\mathbb{F}_p}(\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}/(\overline{s_1}, \overline{s_2},\dots,\overline{s_{16}}))\leq 1825.\]
Then, the ring $\mathcal{A}_K$ is Cohen-Macaulay.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
As in the characteristic zero case, we only need to show that $\mathcal{A}_K$ is a free $K[s_1,s_2,\dots,s_{16}]$-module. Note that since $\mathcal{A}_K=\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_p} K$, it suffices to prove the required claim for $K=\mathbb{F}_p$ which we do below.

Fix a set $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ of size at most $1825$ such that $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ is generated by $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ as a $\mathbb{F}_p[s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16}]$-module. Lift the elements of $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}$, where $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is the ring of $p$-adic integers. Using a similar argument as the one in the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:upper} we get that $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}$ is generated as a $\mathbb{Z}_p[s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16}]$-module by at most $1825$ elements. We can invert $p$ to get that the $\mathbb{Q}_p[s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16}]$-module $ \mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{Q}_p}$ is free of rank $1825$ by Theorem~\ref{main:thm}. Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ must have size exactly $1825$. Furthermore, since $\mathbb{Z}_p[s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16}]$ is torsion-free, we get that $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}$ is a free $\mathbb{Z}_p[s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16}]$-module of rank $1825$. Going modulo $p$, we get that $\mathcal{A}_{\mathbb{F}_p}$ is a free $\mathbb{F}_p[s_1,s_2,\dots, s_{16}]$-module of rank $1825$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
The ring $\mathcal{A}_K$ is Cohen-Macaulay for all but finitely many $p$. Furthermore, $\mathcal{C}_K$ is reduced whenever it is Cohen-Macaulay.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The argument for Cohen-Macaulayness is given above. This along with the fact that $\mathcal{C}_K$ is generically reduced proves reducedness when $K$ is algebraically closed. For general $K$, we note that any nilpotent in $\mathcal{A}_K$ naturally also embeds into $\mathcal{A}_{\overline{K}}$ as a nilpotent, and thus, we conclude that $\mathcal{C}_K$ is reduced.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:perm}
The permutation $\sigma$ defined at the beginning of Section~\ref{sec:sop} was chosen so that for each $1\leq i\leq 14$, the commutator $[b_i,b_{\sigma(i)}]\neq 0$. In fact, each $[b_i,b_{\sigma(i)}]$ is a non-zero scalar multiple of a distinct $b_j$. Therefore, the permutation $\sigma$ could be thought of as a Lie theoretic analog of a complete mapping (see, for example, \cite{Hall}).

This permutation was found by playing around with the above commutator matrix, attempting to select $14$ entries so that there is one in each row and each column. The above property of the permutation ensures that when we substitute $x_i=y_{\sigma(i)}$ in the $14$ quadratic equations $Q_k(x,y)$ defining the scheme $\mathcal{C}$, each of them ends up with exactly one square term. For example, we observe that:
\[(Q_1)_{y_i\mapsto x_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}}=x_3x_{12}-x_9^2 - x_5x_8+x_{11}x_{14} + 2x_6x_7-2x_3x_{12}-x_6x_7 +x_4x_{13}+x_2x_8-x_{13}x_{14},\]
etc. Heuristically, we expect this to be one of the reasons why the above permutation led to a faster Gr\"obner basis computation compared to other options we tried.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
